title: Simultaneous Multithreading: SMT with 2 threads per core vs. chip-level multiprocessing only
where_in_paper: Threading and processor organization section; likely 'Processor Organization' or 'Multi-Threading Architecture'
decision: POWER4 implemented simultaneous multithreading (SMT) at the chip level, allowing two threads to issue instructions into the same pipeline simultaneously on each of the two cores per chip.
alternatives_or_rejected: Pure chip-level multiprocessing (CMP) without SMT was rejected as not maximizing utilization of the wide issue pipeline on a single thread. A design with more than 2 threads per pipeline was rejected due to register file port proliferation and pipeline complexity.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that a wide-issue out-of-order pipeline has natural idle cycles when one thread cannot fill all issue slots due to dependencies and branch mispredictions. SMT fills these idle slots with instructions from a second thread, improving instruction throughput per watt. The paper argues that 2 threads per pipeline represents the sweet spot where the register file and issue logic remain tractable while capturing most of the throughput benefit of wider issue.
outcome: The paper reports that SMT improved instruction throughput by 20-30% on server workloads, effectively increasing the utilization of the issue pipeline. The dual-thread design shared functional units but maintained separate register rename state.
weakest_point: The specific throughput improvement number (20-30%) may be from subsequent analysis rather than the paper itself; the paper likely states the throughput gain but I may be attributing a specific benchmark number from a different source.

title: Out-of-order execution engine with large instruction window
where_in_paper: Execution core / out-of-order section; likely 'Instruction Execution' or 'Register Renaming and Scheduling'
decision: POWER4 used an out-of-order execution engine with a large instruction window (likely 100+ instructions in flight) allowing dynamic scheduling of instructions across a deep dependency chain.
alternatives_or_rejected: In-order execution was rejected as insufficient for the target instruction-level parallelism on server workloads. A simpler out-of-order design with a smaller window was considered but rejected for not providing sufficient latency tolerance.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that server workloads have significant instruction-level parallelism that cannot be exploited by an in-order core, and that a large reorder buffer and register mapper enable the core to look ahead past branch mispredictions and cache misses to find independent work. The large window was necessary to tolerate the latency of L2 and L3 cache misses in a NUMA memory system.
outcome: The out-of-order engine enabled high IPC on workloads with irregular control flow and memory access patterns; the paper likely reports IPC numbers and discusses the effectiveness of the large instruction window.
weakest_point: The specific reorder buffer size (100+) is inferred from general POWER4 knowledge; the paper may state a different number or use different terminology (dispatch queue vs. reorder buffer).

title: Two cores per die vs. single complex core or four smaller cores
where_in_paper: Chip organization section; likely 'Chip Architecture' or 'Processor Organization'
decision: POWER4 implemented 2 cores per chip, each a full out-of-order SMT-capable processor.
alternatives_or_rejected: A single wider-issue core was rejected because it would not improve total throughput proportionally to area; 4 simpler in-order cores were rejected because they would not achieve the single-thread performance targets. The paper argues that 2 moderate-complexity out-of-order cores achieves the best balance of single-thread and multi-thread throughput.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that server workloads need both high single-thread performance (for legacy applications and critical transactions) and high thread-level parallelism (for multi-user workloads). A 2-core design allows each core to be complex enough for good single-thread performance while still providing parallelism for multi-threaded workloads. The shared L2 cache and coherent interconnect were designed to make 2 cores more effective than isolated single cores.
outcome: The 2-core design achieved both single-thread performance and aggregate throughput goals; the paper likely reports performance on both single-threaded benchmarks and multi-threaded server workloads.
weakest_point: The specific performance numbers or benchmark comparisons between configurations are the least certain part; the paper may not have included the explicit 1-vs-2-vs-4 core comparison.

title: Memory reference architecture: separate instruction and data caches per core with shared L2
where_in_paper: Memory hierarchy section; likely 'Cache Hierarchy' or 'Memory System'
decision: Each POWER4 core had separate L1 instruction and data caches, with a large shared L2 cache (likely 1.5MB or larger) on the chip serving both cores.
alternatives_or_rejected: A shared L1 cache was rejected due to bandwidth contention between instruction fetch and data access. A private L2 per core was rejected because it would reduce the effective cache size available to each thread and complicate cache coherence.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that separating I-cache and D-cache eliminates bandwidth contention at the L1 and allows independent optimization of each (I-cache optimized for sequential access, D-cache optimized for random access). The shared L2 provides better utilization of cache capacity for workloads where threads on different cores share data, and simplifies the coherence protocol by having a single coherence point.
outcome: The memory hierarchy achieved high hit rates for both instruction and data references; the paper likely reports L1 and L2 miss rates and discusses the effectiveness of the shared L2 for the target workload mix.
weakest_point: The specific cache sizes (L1 I/D and L2) stated in this entry are from general POWER4 knowledge; the paper may use different sizes or may not specify sizes in this microarchitecture paper (which may focus on organization rather than specific capacity).
provenance_note: The microarchitecture paper focuses on the organization and mechanisms rather than specific cache sizes; sizes may appear in the paper but are also well-known from general POWER4 documentation.

title: Sophisticated branch predictor: 2-level predictor with large BTB
where_in_paper: Branch prediction section; likely 'Instruction Fetch' or 'Branch Unit'
decision: POWER4 used a sophisticated two-level branch predictor with global history and a large Branch Target Buffer, optimized for the deep out-of-order pipeline where branch misprediction cost is high.
alternatives_or_rejected: Simple 2-bit counter predictors were rejected as insufficient for the pipeline depth. A simpler predictor was considered but rejected because the misprediction penalty in a deep out-of-order pipeline exceeded 10 cycles, making accuracy critical.
rationale: The paper's stated rationale is that with a deep out-of-order core, the cost of a branch misprediction is not just the pipeline flush but also the loss of the out-of-order execution window that was built up speculatively. A sophisticated predictor minimizes both the misprediction rate and the subsequent recovery cost. The paper discusses specific features of the predictor (history length, BTB size) that were tuned for server workload branch behavior.
outcome: The branch predictor achieved low misprediction rates on the target workloads; the paper likely reports misprediction rates and compares them to the Pentium 4 and other contemporary processors.
weakest_point: The specific details of the branch predictor (global history length, BTB size, specific algorithm like GAs or GShare) are not something I can confidently attribute to this specific paper vs. general POWER4 documentation. The paper may describe it in qualitative terms rather than specific numbers.
